Pompeii's Graffiti Captures Every Joke, Boast and Argument of an Ancient Roman City Frozen in Time
Graffiti scribbled on a wall in the ancient Roman city of Pompeii
Nearly 2,000 years ago, the ancient Roman cities of Pompeii , Herculaneum and Stabiae bustled with merchants, farmers and families going about their daily lives. Unbeknownst to them, Mount Vesuvius , a still-active volcano that rises above the Bay of Naples in southern Italy, was beginning to stir. A catastrophe was brewing in the Pompeians’ backyard.
To the locals, however, it was just another morning in 79 C.E.
On the day of the infamous disaster, Vesuvius started erupting around noon, sending a towering column of gases, ash and rock fragments into the sky. Author and administrator Pliny the Younger , who was living in the port city of Misenum with his uncle, the naturalist Pliny the Elder , at the time, recorded one of the few eyewitness accounts of the devastation. In his view , the volcanic plume “more closely resembled a pine tree than anything else.”
Heavy pumice and ash rained down from above, crushing roofs and filling courtyards . Later, fast-moving pyroclastic flows rushed down the volcano. Some victims died of asphyxiation ; others were killed instantly by the extreme heat . Among the dead was Pliny the Elder, who was overcome while attempting to rescue friends in Stabiae.
By nightfall the following day , Pompeii was gone, buried under roughly 20 feet of debris.
Ongoing excavations have  shed new light  on Pompeii’s ancient residents, suggesting the city’s elite  built lavish towers  on top of their villas and relaxed in  private spas .
The  poorest survivors  of Vesuvius’ eruption, meanwhile, returned to Pompeii after the disaster and eked out a living in the ash-covered ruins.
In the mid-18th century, when archaeologists first started excavating Pompeii’s ruins, they discovered traces of everyday life in the form of art and artifacts. Frescoes adorned homes, public spaces and temples. Locals scribbled election notices, market day announcements and gossip on buildings’ walls. They also hurled accusations at each other and exchanged witty verses. Children even scrawled crude likenesses of gladiators they’d seen fighting in the arena.
In Pompeii alone, archaeologists have uncovered more than 11,000 examples of graffiti. Some inscriptions were hurriedly written by passers-by, while others showcased their creators’ artistic skill. Graffiti writers belonged to all walks of life. Shopkeepers, laborers, soldiers and enslaved people alike left their marks.
Pompeian graffiti was essentially an ancient version of today’s social media , acting as a form of communication that enabled ordinary people to create, share and respond to messages within a public space.
This charcoal sketch of gladiators was drawn from memory, not imagination, researchers say.
Journalist Tom Standage , author of Writing on the Wall: Social Media—The First 2,000 Years , has seen some of the most interesting examples of ancient graffiti in Pompeii. He says his favorites are the ones “where several people wrote messages, rather like an internet comment thread.” In one instance, two brothers, Onesimus and Secundus, left each other notes on the wall of a mutual friend. Another time, multiple writers offered their own twists on popular couplets on the wall of a stairwell in the House of Maius Castricius.
“These are examples of public discussions—literally, writing on a friend’s wall ,” Standage says. “There are lots of other examples in history as well, but this is one of the earliest, made possible because the Romans had a reasonably high level of literacy .”
The themes covered in Pompeian graffiti aren’t so different from what people post online today. “There are tales of sexual conquest and unrequited love,” Standage says. “There are restaurant reviews , both good and bad. There are insults, jokes … inspirational quotes and poems.”
Pompeii's Graffiti: An Ancient Form of Social Media
In an email,  Alison Cooley , a historian at the University of Warwick in England, points to a conversation between Successus the weaver and his rival, Severus, who competed for the affection of the barmaid Iris by trading clever insults in their graffiti. “Envious one, why do you get in the way?” Successus asked. “Submit to a handsomer man and one who is being treated very wrongly.” Severus, in turn, retorted, “You love Iris, but she does not love you.”
Standage points out that early archaeologists were “ very sniffy about the graffiti in Pompeii when it was first discovered, because it all seemed so trivial. But that is what gives it its value: It shows us that people are much the same and makes the Romans much more relatable. It gives us a flavor of the lives of ordinary Romans.”
Rebecca Benefiel , a classicist at Washington & Lee University, has cataloged inscriptions from Pompeii and Herculaneum for the Ancient Graffiti Project , an online resource focused on the early Roman Empire. These messages “encompassed a wide range of public and private expression, written across spaces both domestic and civic,” she says. “There were many greetings to friends, verses of poetry, personal names, all over the city.”
This painted campaign inscription suggests the home where it was found belonged to one of the candidate's friends or supporters.
The Campus ad Amphitheatrum , a large multipurpose building with more than 100 columns, boasts the most graffiti of any single building in Pompeii, with more than 400 handwritten inscriptions. Other popular spots for leaving graffiti included brothels , baths and the interior walls of private homes .
According to Benefiel, men left behind more graffiti than women. “But plenty of greetings written to women show that it was expected they could read them,” she explains. “ Women sometimes responded with their own greetings, and a few women wrote longer, touching messages.”
Not all of the notes were personal. Some were political, carefully painted in bright red letters by professional signwriters who drummed up support for candidates in upcoming elections. These dipinti , or painted rather than engraved inscriptions, were akin to sponsored social media posts today.
Cooley says that dipinti “pass on the electoral promises of 2,000 years ago.” She adds, “Candidates aspiring to public office were praised for their good character, financial prudence and for benefits they promised to give to the people of Pompeii,” such as free bread and free shows in the amphitheater.
Graffiti painted on the wall of the House of the Moralist in Pompeii
Jamie Heath via Wikimedia Commons under CC BY-SA 2.0
Some candidates engaged in negative campaigning , using graffiti to question their competitors’ qualifications and associate them with untrustworthy groups. “All the late drinkers ask you to elect Marcus Cerrinius Vatia [as magistrate],” one inscription stated. Another suggested a politician was “supported by the petty thieves.”
In Cooley’s view, dipinti reflected the broader civic discourse of Pompeii. “The painted notices (dipinti) rather than the scratched notices (graffiti) seem more likely to reflect a public conversation, because they deal with political affairs,” she explains. These inscriptions, written in large letters for easy reading, invited passers-by to actively participate in civic life.
Graffiti is more spontaneous and less formal than written sources like ancient scrolls . The inscriptions can be exaggerated or humorous, and these qualities make them unique cultural evidence.
“Even though it is tempting to treat graffiti as historical documents,” Cooley says, “it is crucial to remember that they were opinionated, individual messages. When we read that the gladiator Celadus is ‘ the girls’ idol ,’ this is not some sort of objective fact, but more likely a boastful message written by the gladiator himself.”
Graffiti on the wall of a building in Pompeii
Robot8A via Wikimedia Commons under CC BY-SA 4.0
What makes Pompeii’s graffiti so fascinating is not its age but rather the familiarity of it all.
From painted ads to playful banter, the scribblings on the walls remind people today of the human desire to share thoughts and emotions. “It’s a universal and timeless urge,” says Standage. “The internet has just made it much cheaper and easier, which has both benefits and drawbacks. … There are many motivations for wanting to connect: to share information, to find companionship, to keep up with news, to demonstrate one’s status. But connection is the most fundamental aspect of it.”
The author adds, “It’s a social thing. We are social animals, which is what makes social media technologies, both old and new, so compelling.”
Still, Benefiel points out that ancient Roman graffiti isn’t exactly the same as modern social media. “Graffiti captures the character of a society, so our social media trends are quite different from ancient graffiti of the first century,” she says.
Pompeii's Villa of the Mysteries, as seen from above
ElfQrin via Wikimedia Commons under CC BY-SA 4.0
In a 2018 essay , Benefiel identified friendly greetings, poetry and gladiators as three of the most popular topics covered in Pompeii’s graffiti.
“If one is searching for parallels, poetry in antiquity could correspond with modern music, which of course is a foundational element of much social media now,” Benefiel says. “Gladiator matches were the big social event of the time. Does that compare to fashion or celebrity in our present?”
Two thousand years on, the tools have changed, but humans’ need for connection endures.
Cooley’s favorite piece of graffiti is one that appears multiple times throughout Pompeii. It’s a self-referential joke poking fun at how much writing people have left on the walls: “I admire you, wall, for not having collapsed at having to carry the tedious scribblings of so many writers.”
